passage:
Email 1 — From Hana, School Environment Club, to Dr Amal, community adviser.

Dear Dr Amal,
Our club is organising a recycling campaign for neighbourhood families. We hope to collect used batteries and small electronic devices that must not be placed in ordinary household bins. A local shop has offered to advertise the campaign, but its poster includes a photograph of a student who has not agreed to appear on it. Some members think we should accept the poster because printing another one will cost money. I believe we should ask for permission first. Could you help us explain the issue to the shop without damaging our relationship?

Kind regards,
Hana

Email 2 — From Dr Amal to Hana.

Dear Hana,
You are right to consider the student's wishes. A generous offer does not remove the need for consent. Thank the shop for its support and suggest replacing the photograph with a drawing of a recycling box. Explain that the project is about community responsibility and that showing respect is part of its message. Remember that collecting batteries requires safe storage and an approved company to handle the materials. Before announcing a collection point, ask the municipal environment officer for advice and check which items the contractor can legally accept.

Best wishes,
Dr Amal

Email 3 — From Hana to Dr Amal.

Dear Dr Amal,
We followed your advice. The shop has agreed to a new poster with no personal photograph. The environment officer recommended a covered collection point inside the community centre and asked volunteers not to open or repair any batteries. We have booked the centre for Saturday morning. A licensed collection company will transport the materials after the campaign. Our volunteers can explain the instructions, but only trained adults will handle any damaged items.

We still have a problem with information online. One student shared a message promising that every donated device would be repaired and given to another family. The contractor has not made that promise. We removed the message quickly, but several people had already shared it. What is the fairest way to correct the mistake?

Kind regards,
Hana

Email 4 — From Dr Amal to Hana.

Dear Hana,
Publish a clear correction in the same places where the original announcement appeared. State that reusable items may be assessed, while unsuitable ones will be handled according to the contractor's procedures. Do not blame an individual volunteer publicly; explain what your team has learned and name a contact person who can answer questions. At the event, display a short list of accepted devices and provide a sealed box for questions from visitors.

After the campaign, report how many items were collected and whether the agreed safety instructions were followed. Avoid promising environmental benefits you cannot measure. Integrity means telling people what you know, acknowledging what remains uncertain, and correcting information when necessary. Your club can still run a successful campaign by putting those principles into practice.

Kind regards,
Dr Amal
